slide.title: Test Every AI Formula
slide.body: Formula bar with =SUMIFS(…) · result '0' crossed out in red → '2,220' with teal tick. Small tag: AI-Powered Data Analysis · Lesson 5.

production_notes: Screen demo lesson: record in Google Sheets and in Claude or ChatGPT (free tier) with the fictional clean orders sheet from content.md (A1:G11). Use the exact prompts and formulas from content.md: =SUMIFS(C2:C11, G2:G11, "South") → 0, corrected =SUMIFS(G2:G11, C2:C11, "South") → 2,220; =XLOOKUP(1008, A2:A11, G2:G11, "Not found") → 1,800; =MONTH(B2) → 1; =TEXT(B2, "yyyy-mm") in H2.
If the live AI does not produce the swapped SUMIFS on its own, type the swapped formula shown in content.md for the demo; the narration says 'It returns a SUMIFS formula', which stays true.
[VERSION] XLOOKUP availability in Google Sheets and the location of the locale setting (File > Settings) must be checked against the current interface.

[VERSION] [REGION] [VERIFY] Argument separators and function names depend on locale settings. The narration only says that some locale settings use semicolons; it does not name which locales, and it does not say whether function names are translated. Confirm for the fr, pt and ar versions, and re-record the formula close-ups with semicolons where needed.

Aigerim and the Almaty setting are fictional. Spoken numbers match content.md: South 240 + 180 + 1,800 = 2,220, North 680, West 550; lookup 1008 → 1,800, 1002 → 240, 1010 → 120; H2 2026-01, H6 2026-02, H10 2026-03.

Hook.voiceover: You want total revenue for the South region, but you do not remember the formula. AI can write it in seconds. But a formula that looks right can still give the wrong number.

Explain.voiceover: Last time, we cleaned Mateus's orders sheet. Now we ask AI to write formulas for it, and we test every one.

slide.title: AI-Written Formulas in Google Sheets
slide.body: AI-Powered Data Analysis (No Code) · Lesson 5 of 14

Explain.voiceover: Describe what you need in plain words, and an AI assistant can write the formula. A good request has four parts. Where the data is. What each column contains. What you want. And which tool, because formulas differ between spreadsheet tools.

slide.title: A good formula request
slide.body: 1. Where the data is: A1:G11, headers in row 1 · 2. What each column holds: C = Region, G = Revenue · 3. What you want: total revenue where Region is South · 4. Which tool: Google Sheets

Explain.voiceover: Four functions are useful here. SUMIFS adds numbers that meet conditions. XLOOKUP finds a value in one column and returns the matching value from another. IF gives one result when a condition is true, and another when it is false. And date functions, such as TEXT and MONTH, take out parts of a date.

slide.title: Useful functions
slide.body: SUMIFS: add numbers that meet conditions · XLOOKUP: find a value, return the match · IF: one result if true, another if false · TEXT, MONTH: parts of a date

Explain.voiceover: Always test a new formula on a few rows you can check by hand. If the formula and your hand check agree on three rows, you can trust it much more. And if you do not understand a formula, ask the AI to explain it.
Explain.on_screen_text: Test every formula on three rows

Explain.voiceover: One more thing. In some locale settings, Google Sheets uses semicolons instead of commas between the parts of a formula. If an AI formula shows a parse error, check the separators.

slide.title: Comma or semicolon?
slide.body: =SUMIFS(G2:G11, C2:C11, "South") | =SUMIFS(G2:G11; C2:C11; "South") · Caption: set by the spreadsheet locale. Parse error? Check the separators.

Explain.voiceover: Think of an AI-written formula as a recipe from a friend who has never seen your kitchen. It is usually close, but you still taste the dish before you serve it.
Explain.stock_query: cook tasting sauce with spoon kitchen

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's watch. Aigerim is a finance assistant in Almaty, Kazakhstan. She uses the clean, fictional orders sheet from the last lesson, with ten orders and revenue in US dollars.

slide.title: Aigerim's practice sheet (fictional)
slide.body: Clean 10-row orders table from content.md, columns Order ID | Order Date | Region | Product | Units | Unit Price | Revenue: 1001 2026-01-08 North Notebook pack 20 4 80 · 1002 2026-01-15 South Office chair 2 120 240 · 1003 2026-01-22 West Desk lamp 5 30 150 · 1004 2026-02-03 North Office chair 3 120 360 · 1005 2026-02-11 West Notebook pack 40 4 160 · 1006 2026-02-19 South Desk lamp 6 30 180 · 1007 2026-02-26 North Desk lamp 4 30 120 · 1008 2026-03-04 South Office chair 15 120 1800 · 1009 2026-03-18 West Office chair 2 120 240 · 1010 2026-03-25 North Notebook pack 30 4 120. Caption: Aigerim · Almaty

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, a total by region. She asks the AI for total revenue where region is South. It returns a SUMIFS formula. She types it into cell J2, and the result is zero.
screen_steps: In the AI chat, type: 'My Google Sheets data is in A1:G11, headers in row 1. Column C is Region, column G is Revenue. Write a formula for total revenue where Region is South.'
Show the AI reply: =SUMIFS(C2:C11, G2:G11, "South")
Switch to Google Sheets, click cell J2 and type the formula
Press Enter: J2 shows 0; zoom on the cell

Demonstrate.voiceover: Zero cannot be right. She checks by hand. The South orders are two hundred and forty, one hundred and eighty, and one thousand eight hundred. That makes two thousand two hundred and twenty. The AI swapped the ranges. In SUMIFS, the range to add comes first.
screen_steps: Highlight the three South rows (1002, 1006, 1008) in yellow
Show the hand sum as an overlay: 240 + 180 + 1,800 = 2,220
Click J2 and highlight the two ranges in the formula bar: C2:C11 is first, G2:G11 is second

Demonstrate.voiceover: She puts the revenue range first. Now the result is two thousand two hundred and twenty. She checks North the same way, which gives six hundred and eighty, and West, which gives five hundred and fifty.
screen_steps: Edit J2 to =SUMIFS(G2:G11, C2:C11, "South") and press Enter: 2,220
In J3 enter the same formula with "North": 680
In J4 enter the same formula with "West": 550
Show a small hand-check column beside J2:J4 with green ticks

Demonstrate.voiceover: Second, a lookup. She asks for the revenue of a given order ID. The AI gives an XLOOKUP formula. For order ten oh eight, it returns one thousand eight hundred. She tests order ten oh two, which gives two hundred and forty, and order ten ten, which gives one hundred and twenty. An ID that does not exist returns not found, as expected.
screen_steps: In the AI chat, ask for 'the revenue of a given Order ID'
Show the reply: =XLOOKUP(1008, A2:A11, G2:G11, "Not found")
Enter it in Google Sheets: 1,800; highlight row 1008
Change 1008 to 1002: 240; highlight row 1002
Change to 1010: 120; highlight row 1010
Change to 1099: Not found

Demonstrate.voiceover: Third, a month column for grouping. The AI first suggests the MONTH function, which returns just the number one. So she asks, will this mix January twenty twenty-six with January twenty twenty-seven? It will. The AI suggests a better version with TEXT, which shows the year and the month.
screen_steps: In the AI chat, ask for 'a Month column for grouping'
Show the reply =MONTH(B2); enter it in a spare cell: 1
Type in the chat: 'Will this mix January 2026 with January 2027?'
Show the improved reply: =TEXT(B2, "yyyy-mm")

Demonstrate.voiceover: She types the header Month in H1, puts the formula in H2, and fills it down. She checks three rows. H2 shows twenty twenty-six, zero one. H6 shows twenty twenty-six, zero two. And H10 shows twenty twenty-six, zero three.
screen_steps: Type 'Month' in H1
Enter =TEXT(B2, "yyyy-mm") in H2 and fill down to H11
Zoom on H2 (2026-01), H6 (2026-02) and H10 (2026-03), each next to its date in column B

Demonstrate.voiceover: Finally, she asks the AI to explain the SUMIFS formula step by step, and points to each range as she reads.
screen_steps: In the AI chat, type: 'Explain this formula step by step: =SUMIFS(G2:G11, C2:C11, "South")'
Scroll through the explanation
Switch to the sheet and highlight G2:G11, then C2:C11, then the word "South" as each part is explained

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to accept a formula because it returns a number without an error. A wrong formula often returns a real-looking number, or zero, with no warning. Only a hand check shows it is correct.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: No error does not mean correct

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, describe the data, the columns, what you want and the tool, and AI can write a useful formula. Second, test every AI formula on at least three rows by hand, and correct it if the results differ. Third, ask the AI to explain any formula you do not understand, and watch the separators for your locale.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Where · what · want · which tool. 2. Test on 3 rows by hand; correct if different. 3. Ask AI to explain; check separators for your locale.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will ask Claude or ChatGPT for three formulas: a total by region, a lookup, and a date calculation. Test each one on three rows by hand, and correct any that are wrong. It takes about thirty minutes. Next time, we start week two with asking good questions of your data. See you there.
